basic_info.name: Clinical note omission and hallucination evaluation papers (OmissionBench, arXiv:2608.31016; inference-aware SOAP hallucination judge, arXiv:2604.14829)
basic_info.description: A pair of 2026 evaluation-methodology artifacts that jointly define how to audit AI clinical notes for missing content versus invented content. Artifact one is OmissionBench, home of the paper 'LLM Judges Verify Presence, Not Absence: Omission Blindness in AI Clinical Notes and What Recovers It' (Sebastian Fox, Luke Markham, Ryan Lail, Michael Karotsieris; Composo AI, London; submitted 31 Aug 2026, v1 only): across eight judge designs, LLM judges reliably flag added or altered note content (paired discrimination 0.79-0.94) but sit at near chance on omissions (0.50-0.63), and only restructuring the task - enumerate the facts the transcript establishes, then check each against the note as a closed presence verdict - recovers usable (though partial) omission detection. Artifact two is 'Beyond Literal Summarization: Redefining Hallucination for Medical SOAP Note Evaluation' (Bhavik Vachhani, Kush Shrisvastava, Pranshu Nema, Sai Chiranthan; Augnito Research, India; submitted 16 Apr 2026, v1 only): a purely lexical faithfulness judge scores a 35.2% mean hallucination rate on SOAP notes against a 10.4% human-annotator baseline, while an inference-aware judge using calibrated prompting plus retrieval over SNOMED CT, ICD-10 and drug-equivalence resources drops to 9.1%. The load-bearing fact connecting them is that these are not competing claims but complementary halves of the same measurement problem - the omission paper measures the absence side and cites Vachhani et al. 2026 as 'the one result pointing the other way' among judge-reliability studies, i.e. the only comparator claiming an inference-aware judge can substantially fix the over-flagging side; the Augnito paper measures the commission side and says nothing about omissions. A concurrently released companion census (arXiv:2608.31017, same Composo authors) supplies the production motivation: 31.3% [27.0, 35.6] of 565 notes from three deployed AI scribes carried at least one verified failure, with omission reported by prior human audits as the dominant error class (54%-86.3% of all errors).
basic_info.organization: Artifact one and its companion census: Composo AI (Composo Ltd / Composo AI), London - Sebastian Fox (CEO and co-founder, also the paper's lead author and a medical doctor from Oxford), Luke Markham (CTO and co-founder), Ryan Lail, Michael Karotsieris. Artifact two: Augnito Research, the research group of the clinical-documentation vendor Augnito India Private Limited (Mumbai), with a clinical acknowledgement to Dr. Nikhil Saldanha for manual note verification.
basic_info.country: Two origins: OmissionBench / the omission-blindness paper is from the United Kingdom (Composo AI, headquartered at 3 Waterhouse Square, London EC1N 2SW, with a distributed workforce across the UK and South Africa); the inference-aware hallucination paper is from India (Augnito Research / Augnito India Private Limited, Mumbai). Neither study is India-market-specific in its data: the omission benchmark is built from UK primary-care (PriMock57) and US ambulatory (ACI-Bench) consultations plus authored scenarios, and the Augnito paper uses 100 anonymised physician-patient transcripts across cardiology, dermatology, endocrinology, ENT and family medicine with no stated country of origin.
basic_info.status: research. Both are non-peer-reviewed arXiv preprints as of the verification date. OmissionBench is an actively released benchmark and open harness (no v2 posted; last data version tagged 'factorial-v1'), and its companion census was released on the same day. The Augnito paper is a single v1 preprint that remains contested: an independent T0 machine review on Pith raised two load-bearing objections (no dataset size or validation protocol in the abstract; no evidence that the residual 9% is free of false negatives), the authors replied 'revision: yes' and described additions to a revised manuscript, but no revised arXiv version had appeared and citation listings still showed the item effectively uncited as of 2026-09-16.

technical_features.what_it_does: The two artifacts attack opposite halves of clinical-note fidelity measurement. OmissionBench operationalises the absence question: it is a 500-pair benchmark of single-error note twins (495 pairs in the evaluation set, 293 of them omissions and 202 added-or-altered commission controls, plus 112 verified-clean twins) in which a named fact's primary statement was removed from an otherwise clean note and is known with certainty to be absent, graded by severity and by how much of the removed fact survives elsewhere. It then measures whether a second LLM (the judge) can tell the flawed note from its clean twin and whether, on a single note with no twin available, the judge flags omissions more often than it flags perfect notes. The paper's method contribution is the recovery: instead of asking 'is anything missing?', the judge first enumerates the facts the transcript establishes and then returns a closed present/partial/absent verdict per fact, with a note-level decision rule over those verdicts. The Augnito artifact addresses the commission side: it defines what should and should not count as hallucination in SOAP notes (five tiers from direct statement through paraphrase, trade/generic equivalence and clinical inference to speculative overreach and contradiction), then compares a lexical, inference-unaware judge against an inference-aware judge whose prompt is clinically calibrated and augmented by retrieval from SNOMED CT, ICD-10 and drug-name resources, with a retained hard safety floor on unsupported medications, doses, procedures and contradictions.
technical_features.architecture: OmissionBench paper - an evaluation harness plus a constructed benchmark, not a clinical system. The benchmark is built as a single-edit pair factory: fact sheets are authored per consultation from the transcript alone (never from the reference note), two models from different families grade each fact's severity against a written rubric and the lower grade is taken, removal attempts are verified by a cross-family adversarial panel, and pairs are allocated so that trace-by-severity combinations are balanced. The judge roster is an eighteen-configuration, eight-design ablation crossing what the judge is asked to check (faithfulness only versus faithfulness plus completeness), how it answers (binary verdict versus 0-10 score) and how many times (single call versus an eight-sample ensemble combined by a winsorised mean). Two recovery designs are then compared: a two-stage enumerate-then-check pipeline (extraction call that never sees the note, then one keyed present-or-absent verdict per fact) and a three-stage pipeline that adds a critic audit which drops weak facts and grades severity, plus a quote-verified second look on any fact flagged absent; and a single GEPA-evolved prompt that executes the same enumerate-then-check instruction inside one call under a high reasoning budget and a clean-note calibration. Augnito paper - a two-stage LLM-as-judge framework. Stage 1 is a strict fact-checking prompt ('if not directly stated, mark HALLUCINATED') applied claim-by-claim. Stage 2 replaces it with a clinically calibrated prompt plus a retrieval-augmented knowledge layer: each note claim is used as a query against a knowledge base assembled from SNOMED CT (terminology and concept relationships), ICD-10 (diagnostic classification) and open-source pharmacological resources (generic/trade-name equivalence), and the retrieved context is appended to the judge's input. Stage 2 additionally enforces cross-section verification (a claim may be grounded anywhere in the four SOAP sections), a non-negotiable synonym rule for trade versus generic drug names, and a five-step chain of thought that makes hallucination the verdict of last resort.
technical_features.inputs: OmissionBench paper - benchmark construction consumes consultation transcripts from three strata: PriMock57 (UK primary care; 57 consultations, 53 usable), ACI-Bench (US ambulatory; 48 consultations, 45 usable) and authored consultations including a trap-blind stratum written without knowledge of the trap schema, plus per-consultation fact sheets, a fact-site map and severity grades. The pipeline at run time consumes a transcript and a note. Augnito paper - 100 anonymised physician-patient transcripts spanning cardiology, dermatology, endocrinology, ENT and family medicine, each paired with an LLM-generated SOAP note; the Stage 2 judge additionally consumes retrieved terminology/ontology/drug context per claim.
technical_features.outputs: OmissionBench paper - no clinical document. It emits per-note and per-fact judgements (present/partial/absent verdicts with, in the three-stage tier, a severity grade and a supporting quote for flags), paired-discrimination scores, detection and false-alarm rates, and cost records; the released artifacts are the graded pairs, the fact-site map, the severity grades with both graders' verdicts, the transcripts in derived form, per-consultation fact sheets, census findings with transcript-side evidence, every benchmark judge run's judgements and manifests, and clinician sitting records. Augnito paper - hallucination-rate metrics (mean rate per evaluation condition) and a five-tier claim-classification breakdown; it does not release a dataset, code or a FHIR artifact.
technical_features.standards_compliance: Neither artifact conforms to, claims, or validates any clinical document or interoperability standard. OmissionBench references SNOMED CT only indirectly, through one of its public corpus strata (ACI-Bench) and through cited prior work; its benchmark fact identities are free text, and its outputs are evaluation scores rather than coded or FHIR resources. The Augnito paper uses SNOMED CT for terminology and concept relationships, ICD-10 for diagnostic classification and unspecified open-source drug knowledge only as the judge's retrieval grounding - none of it appears in an output binding, profile or validation step, and no FHIR R4/R4B, HL7 IPS, LOINC or NRCeS profile is mentioned anywhere. There is no conformance statement to audit in either paper; the standards are evaluation inputs, not output contracts.
technical_features.offline_capability: Neither artifact is designed for offline operation and both depend on hosted frontier models. Every judge, extractor, auditor and reflector in the omission study is a pinned commercial API model (OpenAI GPT-5.4 as the primary judge, OpenAI GPT-5.5 for extraction/reflection, Anthropic Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 4.8, and Google Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview as the second judge family), with costs quoted per note from provider usage receipts; the Augnito judge is likewise an unspecified hosted LLM, and its Stage 2 retrieval layer assumes access to SNOMED CT, ICD-10 and drug knowledge bases. The important nuance for a constrained deployment is that the omission paper's *method* - enumerate visible facts, then perform closed per-fact presence checks, decompose rather than ask one holistic question - is model-agnostic and the paper itself notes that decomposition beats a single clever prompt; nothing in the method requires a frontier model, but no CPU/offline realisation is demonstrated or measured, and no local storage, encryption, sync or store-and-forward mechanism is described in either work.
technical_features.languages_supported: English only in both primary studies. OmissionBench's public strata and authored scenarios are English (UK and US consultations), all prompts, judges and clinician sittings are English, and no Hindi, Devanagari or Hinglish capability is reported. The Augnito study is English-only in its 100 transcripts, prompts and rubric, despite Augnito as a vendor operating substantially in Indian clinical practice. Neither paper evaluates code-mixed or Indian-language clinical text; a cited comparator (Dahlberg et al. 2026) does test deletions across three languages, but that is external to these artifacts.
technical_features.deployment_model: Both are API-dependent research/evaluation deployments, not kiosk or on-device systems. The omission harness runs as a cloud evaluation job against pinned commercial endpoints, with measured per-note costs; the released code and dataset are intended to be re-run by other teams against their own or vendor notes, and the paper notes that the pipeline's per-consultation stages (extraction, audit) are cached and amortised across notes, which is precisely a server-side deployment pattern. The Augnito framework is a judge configuration applied to hosted models. Neither reports local hardware requirements, and neither is positioned for a ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: Omission paper, on the 495-pair evaluation set: paired discrimination (tie-adjusted probability that the flawed note scores below its own clean twin, where 0.500 is a coin flip) is 0.79-0.94 on added-or-altered content but only 0.50-0.63 on omissions across the eight designs. On single notes, no design flags omissions reliably more often than perfect notes: threshold-free area under the detection curve runs 0.503-0.575, and swept to a 10% false-alarm ceiling the best scored design reaches 8.3% detection at 6.5% false alarms, a gap that does not clear its own noise. The two recovery methods: (a) the per-fact enumerate-then-check pipeline detects 24.6% of omission notes at a 2.7% false-alarm rate, and its flags name the missing fact and its severity; (b) the single GEPA-evolved prompt detects 36.9% at 6.2% false alarms (p = 0.002, consultations as the unit) at roughly a tenth of the pipeline's measured cost per note at one note per consultation, and on the held-out confirmation run catches 32.1% [24.7, 40.5] of 131 held-out omission notes at a 2.1% false-alarm rate. On the 261 real vendor notes from the companion census every operating point moves: detection roughly doubles (pipeline 51.7%, evolved prompt 85.1%) with false alarms rising 8.3-fold and 7.1-fold (to 22.4% and 44.2%), and on census notes carrying a verified omission three quarters of the pipeline's flags name the very fact the census panel verified. On the same benchmark, the best monolithic judge given the pipeline's own audited fact list and a high reasoning budget still reaches only 0.699 paired discrimination versus the two-stage pipeline's 0.786. The named open failure is restatement: an omission whose fact survives as an explicit or paraphrased second mention elsewhere in the note defeats both recovery routes, and the paper measures the supply of such cases four ways (32.0% of recorded facts stated more than once, 44% of complete removals failing verification, ~a quarter of sampled census omission refusals turning on a restatement, and 90.2% of surviving restatements sitting under a different heading). Augnito paper: mean hallucination rate 35.2% under the Stage 1 inference-unaware (lexical) judge, 9.1% under the Stage 2 inference-aware judge, against a human-annotator baseline of 10.4%; the Stage 1-to-human gap is 24.8 percentage points and Stage 2 closes it to 1.3 points. Stage-by-stage, Stage 1 systematically flagged diagnostic inference (e.g. GERD or peptic ulcer disease inferred from a symptom cluster), terminology translation (e.g. 'dyspnoea on exertion' for 'gets breathless when climbing stairs') and standard-of-care plan entries (e.g. ordering HbA1c), while both stages agreed on genuine Tier 4-5 fabrications and contradictions.
performance_metrics.latency: [uncertain] Not reported by either paper. The omission paper states explicitly that no latency was measured: the harness records token receipts, cost and a completion timestamp per call but no per-call wall-clock duration, 'so no latency figure exists and none should be inferred from the timestamps'. The Augnito paper reports no latency, throughput or time-to-judgement at all, and neither paper reports the hardware or endpoint loading behind its API calls. Latency is therefore unknown for both and must be measured locally if the OmissionBench method is reused.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: No local hardware footprint is stated for either artifact because both run against hosted frontier model APIs. The omission study pins: openai/gpt-5.4 as the primary judge (temperature 1.0, reasoning effort none, 1,024 max output tokens), openai/gpt-5.5 for extraction and reflection (temperature 1.0, high reasoning effort except medium in census work), anthropic/claude-opus-5 (temperature 1.0, medium effort, 16,000 tokens) and anthropic/claude-opus-4.8 in the verification panel, with google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview as the second judge family (temperature 1.0, reasoning effort minimal - the endpoint refuses to disable reasoning). Costs, not RAM, are the constraint: per note at one note per consultation the evolved prompt is USD 0.046, the RAGAS-style coverage recipe USD 0.03-0.07, the two-stage pipeline USD 0.094 (USD 0.028 amortised across a consultation's notes) and the three-stage pipeline USD 0.45 (USD 0.140 amortised), of which the severity audit is 71%. The Augnito framework runs on an unspecified hosted judge plus retrieval services and publishes no resource figures.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Omission benchmark: 500 graded single-error pairs (495 in the evaluation set), split into 293 omission pairs (150 complete-removal, 86 fragment-trace, 57 restatement-trace) and 202 added-or-altered controls, over 112 evaluation consultations and 112 clean twins; a 151-pair held-out subset over 47 consultations (131 omission pairs, 47 clean twins) never seen by any optimiser; 141-142 consultation transcripts across four strata; a build costing USD 7.29 over 173 calls (USD 0.026 per pair), with 277 pairs planned from 177 target facts; and a per-note fact load of 39.2 facts extracted and 37.6 retained after audit, giving 7,443 per-fact verdicts in one confirmation run. Augnito study: 100 anonymised physician-patient transcripts across five-plus specialties, one LLM-generated SOAP note per transcript, and one human-annotator baseline condition. Companion census: 142 consultations, 565 notes (282/141/142 because one product writes two note styles), twelve discovery passes proposing 13,678 candidate errors, 5,898 passing an importance filter to an adversarial two-model panel, and 618 verified findings.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Omission paper - the protocol is unusually explicit and adversarial. Ground truth is built from the transcript rather than borrowed from clinician reference notes, because the authors first audited those references and found 100% of usable PriMock notes (53/53) and 100% of usable ACI-Bench notes (45/45) carry at least one material discrepancy with their own transcript, at means of 10.7 and 7.1 discrepancies per note. Benchmark pairs are single-edit (deletion only), severity-graded by two different-family models on a written rubric with the lower grade taken, and removal attempts are verified by a cross-family panel (only 71 of 126 complete-removal attempts survive, versus 114 of 151 trace-leaving removals). Judging uses a pinned primary model family for all headline results with a second family for replication; repeat runs collapse to a per-note majority before significance testing, bootstrap resampling is at the consultation rather than the note, paired comparisons use an exact McNemar test with Holm correction and the one unpaired comparison Boschloo's exact test, and Wilson intervals are used for proportions. Human validation runs through the study: a physician author validated 70 items on 14 August 2026 across six stages (three structurally blinded) and sided with the pipeline on 10 of 10 disagreements with the best monolithic judge (p = 0.002), and an independent clinician graded the severity rubric blind in a 24-item sitting on 17 August 2026, agreeing to within a grade. The paper discloses that the authors build evaluation tooling commercially, that the recommended pipeline is their own design, and that the reference judges include their own production faithfulness judge. Augnito paper - the protocol is a same-output, two-judge-condition comparison on 100 transcripts scored against a human-annotator baseline; it is explicitly not peer-reviewed, the dataset and prompts are not released, the number of SOAP notes and the inter-rater reliability of the human baseline are not reported in the paper, and the residual 9.1% is asserted rather than independently adjudicated. An independent T0 review (Pith, 10 May 2026) raised exactly these two as load-bearing objections and asked for multi-expert classification and a false-negative assessment; the authors responded 'revision: yes' claiming added detail and a labelled held-out comparison, but no revised arXiv version exists, so the headline numbers remain vendor-reported and unreplicated.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: These papers are the direct evidence base for Module C's evaluation harness and for its decision to exclude an LLM from summary generation in v1. The omission paper supplies the single most important harness requirement: an evaluator that asks 'is anything missing?' will not work, because judges verify presence and sit at chance on absence (paired 0.50-0.63 on omissions against 0.79-0.94 on invented content; single-note AUC 0.50-0.58). The correct fix is structural, not a better prompt - enumerate the facts the bundle establishes (from Module A's slots and Module B's FHIR extracts), then make one closed present/absent check per fact and decide on the verdicts - which is exactly the shape of the per-view field-recall plus explicit omission check already specified for Module C's eval harness (doc/18 C6). The paper also warns about the exact blind spot most dangerous for a doctor-facing summary: content that is present but misplaced. Restatement-trace omissions (90.2% of surviving restatements sit under a different heading) defeat both recovery methods, and the authors name per-section coverage scoring as the structural attack - i.e. Module C should check coverage per OPConsultRecord section, not per note, so a SOCRATES fact dropped from the history section but echoed in the assessment is still counted as a failure. Finally, the paper's cost ladder (USD 0.046-0.45 per note, cloud APIs) and the census finding that the dominant production failure class is allergy/medication information (directly relevant to the OPConsultRecord medication and allergy slices) reinforce that Module C should not rely on a hosted judge at inference time. The Augnito paper supplies the counterweight that prevents the harness from being wrongly strict: a lexical grounding rule inflates hallucination to 35.2% against a 10.4% human baseline because it cannot distinguish legitimate clinical normalisation (paraphrase, lay-to-medical translation, cross-section safety inference) from fabrication. For Module C this is the measurement argument for a per-line provenance contract - every rendered line carries a canon field id, so a 'fabrication' is an unresolvable provenance pointer rather than a semantic judgement - and it justifies wiring the same inference-aware criteria into any phase-2 LLM lane and into the judge used to score bilingual rendering. Because the Augnito result is vendor-authored and contested, it is a design input to be adopted with its caveats, not a settled number.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) the enumerate-then-check restructuring as the core of the Module C harness - build the expected-fact list from the HistoryBundle (not from the generated summary), then assert each fact present, partial or absent, and decide on the verdicts rather than on a holistic score; (2) per-fact flags that name the missing item and its severity, because that is what makes an omission report actionable for the physician attestation step; (3) per-section coverage scoring against the OPConsultRecord sections as the named countermeasure to restatement-trace omissions; (4) severity grading against a written, clinician-validated rubric, with an independent clinician blind-grading the rubric (the omission paper shows this is achievable with one author-adjacent and one independent clinician); (5) the Augnito five-tier claim taxonomy and its retained safety floor as the definition of a genuine fabrication in any LLM-assisted lane - unsupported medication/dose/frequency/duration, a diagnosis neither stated nor inferable, an unmentioned procedure, or a direct contradiction; (6) the Augnito cross-section verification rule (evidence anywhere in the bundle grounds a rendered line) and its non-negotiable trade/generic equivalence rule for medication rendering; (7) audit the same failed-agent behaviour it exposes: never let a summary invent or upgrade identity details, dates, or examination findings (the census found history rewritten as performed examination on telephone consultations that could not have contained one), which maps directly onto Module C's elicit-never-diagnose and provenance rules. Reject: (1) relying on a monolithic LLM judge for omission QA - the paper's own null across five remedy families (wording, criteria, answer format, voting, GEPA prompt optimisation) shows prompt work moves the operating point without creating usable detection; (2) treating a lexical-faithfulness hallucination rate as a quality metric, since the Augnito result shows it over-penalises valid clinical normalisation; (3) cloud frontier judges (GPT-5.4/5.5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1) as a kiosk-time dependency, given the offline and India-residency constraints and the per-note costs; (4) quoting the 35%/9% figures as settled - the 9.1% residual is unvalidated, unreplicated and vendor-claimed; (5) the 'flag anything below 10' evolved-prompt calibration, which the authors themselves say is a behaviour of a particular corpus and judge and must be re-established per deployment; and (6) any design that produces a holistic score rather than named, per-field verdicts.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Both artifacts are non-peer-reviewed preprints and, in the Augnito case, contested by an independent review. Omission paper limits: headline judgements come from one judge model family (a second family reproduces the asymmetry but single-note claims are scoped to the first family); reasoning effort is not matched tier-for-tier across families, and the second family's endpoint refuses a no-reasoning setting, so family and deliberation are confounded in those comparisons; the benchmark's own construction could be circular because the pipeline enumerates facts much as construction did, which the authors rebut with blind extraction recovery (99.4% of human-authored facts on kept sheets), the RAGAS-style recipe landing inside the pipeline's range, independent replication by DeLucia et al., and the blinded physician adjudication - but the concern is acknowledged rather than eliminated; no method comes close to solving omission detection (best held-out 32.1% at 2.1% false alarms), and restatement-trace omissions defeat both methods; thresholds do not transfer from the constructed benchmark to real vendor notes (detection and false alarms both rise sharply, and the clean-note calibration must be re-established per deployment); no latency was measured; the authors build and sell evaluation tooling and recommend their own pipeline, a disclosed competing interest. Augnito paper limits: only v1 exists after a reviewer request for revision; the dataset (100 transcripts), the SOAP-note generation model, the judge model, and the human-annotation protocol and inter-rater reliability are not released or fully specified; the central claim that the residual 9.1% reflects only genuine safety concerns is asserted qualitatively, with no false-negative risk assessment or independent multi-expert adjudication, which is precisely the objection that remains open; the study measures only commission errors and says nothing about omissions (so it cannot be used to argue the omission problem is solved); and the vendor affiliation creates a direct incentive to show that the vendor's own documentation output is not really hallucinating. Downstream ecosystem risk: the omission paper lists several concurrent 2026 studies with partially conflicting directions (Hussain et al. plus F1 on mental-health data; Bergman et al.'s vendor-authored judge-validation and five-country paired studies; Dahlberg et al.'s systematic review), so the judge-reliability picture is still moving and any Module C metric set should be treated as provisional.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: Neither artifact is a competitor - both are evaluation methodology, so they do not erode MediKiosk's offline, India-residency, NRCeS-conformant-emission, per-field-provenance or physician-attestation differentiation; if anything they sharpen the case for it. The omission paper is a UK/US, cloud-API, English-only benchmark of ambient-scribe note twins whose most useful warning for MediKiosk is that even a good judge cannot see omissions, which strengthens the argument for a deterministic renderer that emits a physician-facing totality (every expected field either filled or explicitly marked absent/not-elicited) rather than a prose note whose completeness must be inferred. The Augnito paper is authored by an Indian clinical-documentation vendor (Augnito India Private Limited, Mumbai) and is the only India-origin artifact in this cluster, but it is a methodology study - it reports judge behaviour on English SOAP notes, releases no kiosk, no offline path, no Indic handling and no FHIR/NRCeS mapping, and its contested 35%/9% result is a caution against lexical scoring rather than a product. Where MediKiosk differs is decisive: it renders against a frozen HistoryBundle with per-line canon field ids (so 'fabrication' becomes a resolvable provenance pointer, not a semantic judgement), it must run offline on a ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk (so neither cloud judge is deployable at kiosk time), it emits NRCeS OPConsultRecord with SNOMED CT/LOINC/NAMASTE bindings (neither artifact produces or validates any coded or FHIR artifact), it must render bilingually in Hindi/Devanagari or Hinglish (both studies are English-only), and it is elicit-never-diagnose (the Augnito paper's Tier 3 'legitimate clinical inference' explicitly includes diagnostic inference, which Module C must not emit). In short, these papers supply the measurement language and two named failure modes - omission blindness and lexical over-penalisation - that MediKiosk can convert into a stronger, deterministic, provenance-carrying eval contract than either provides.

business_info.license: Omission paper artifacts: the OmissionBench dataset is released under CC BY 4.0 (huggingface.co/datasets/ComposoAI/OmissionBench, data version 'factorial-v1', with a DataCite DOI minted against the released revision); the harness, prompts and judge configurations at github.com/composo-ai/omission-bench are under the MIT licence and archived to Zenodo under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22160954; the arXiv paper itself is under arXiv's perpetual non-exclusive licence (not CC). Vendor note text is withheld from the release for licence reasons, with the released findings quoting only the transcript side. Augnito paper: the paper is CC BY 4.0; no dataset, code, prompts or model are released, so there is no artefact licence.
business_info.pricing: No published pricing for either research artifact; both papers, the OmissionBench dataset and the omission harness are free. Composo is a commercial vendor whose enterprise evaluation platform is sold through 2-4 week engagements with custom quotes rather than public list pricing, so the underlying commercial product behind the omission research is quote-only. Augnito is a commercial clinical-documentation vendor (doctor-side dictation and ambient EMR) whose product pricing is likewise not published; the paper itself is a free preprint with no commercial terms.
business_info.funding: [uncertain] Composo: USD 2.0M pre-seed (seed round dated 17 Dec 2024) led by the British AI pre-seed fund Twin Path Ventures with participation from JVH Ventures and EWOR (which had previously backed Composo through its accelerator); reported customers include Accenture, Palantir and McKinsey. The research is the company's own funded work and the paper declares a competing interest ('the authors build evaluation tooling commercially'). Augnito Research: the paper names no funding source or grant, and no funding figure for Augnito India Private Limited's research activities was found in this sweep; Augnito is an established Indian medical-voice/EMR vendor but its corporate funding history was not verified here.
business_info.commercial_status: Mixed and asymmetric. Composo is a venture-backed commercial company (London, founded 2023, ~5 employees, SOC 2 Type II, EU data residency and on-prem/VPC options) that has published an open benchmark and open harness as a credibility and lead-generation asset while its paid product is a managed LLM-evaluation quality layer; the omission and census papers are the company's marketing-through-evidence. The Augnito paper is unpaid-looking research from a commercial Indian clinical-documentation vendor, published as a free CC BY 4.0 preprint with no accompanying product release, and it carries an implicit commercial interest in showing that current hallucination benchmarks over-penalise legitimate clinical documentation of the kind its products generate.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: For the omission/hallucination evaluation niche specifically: MED-OMIT (Schumacher et al., arXiv:2311.08303) is the direct ancestor of fact-enumeration for omission measurement and the omission paper says what is new is that restructuring recovers judge detection and how to act on the verdicts; CARE (Bedi et al. 2026) engineers calibrated hallucination and omission flags together and reaches the same 'separate detectors' conclusion by design; RAGAS (Es et al. 2024) supplies the per-fact coverage lineage and is run as a comparator; AbsenceBench (Fu et al., 2025) established the underlying absence-detection gap for language models generally and is explicitly noted as the setting this paper makes harder (semantic absence, no side-by-side original, medical domain); MEDEC (Ben Abacha et al., 2025) measures judges on commission errors; DeLucia et al. 2026 independently reports the clinical-completeness-judge null; Dahlberg et al. 2026 is a systematic review and benchmark of note-evaluation methods; Hussain et al. 2026 blends human and LLM expertise for hallucination and omission detection in mental-health chat; Bergman et al. 2026a validates automated documentation-error judges and 2026b runs a five-country paired note-quality study, both vendor-authored. For Composo's parent market (LLM evaluation platforms) the named competitors are Agenta, Freeplay, Humanloop and LangSmith. For the Augnito paper the nearest competitors are the same note-evaluation line plus the Omi Health SOAP note safety benchmark (safety-weighted composite with hallucination and omission as first-class metrics) and the CREOLA/Tortus clinical-review framework.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: None clinical. Neither artifact integrates with an EHR/HIS, an ABDM gateway role (HIP/HIU/PHR), a health locker, or any messaging or terminology service. The omission harness integrates only with pinned commercial model endpoints and with public research corpora (PriMock57, ACI-Bench) and, for the real-world run, with the companion census's three anonymised vendor-scribe products. The Augnito framework integrates with a hosted judge and with SNOMED CT, ICD-10 and drug-knowledge retrieval sources, but publishes no endpoint or service contract. There is no pathway in either work by which Module C could wire directly into ABDM.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: The surrounding ecosystem is converging on the exact asymmetry these papers name, which is a tailwind for Module C's likely direction but also means the methodology is fluid. Between April and September 2026 several independent studies reached related conclusions: OmissionBench (Aug 2026) and its census; DeLucia et al. (Apr 2026) on completeness-judge disagreement; Dahlberg et al. (Jul 2026, AI in Medicine) on judges responding to deletions at half their response to modifications; Hussain et al. (Apr 2026) blending human and LLM detection; Bergman et al. (Aug 2026) showing clinician-to-clinician agreement on judge flags is only fair and that a calibrated reviewer found 24.4% errors where clinician adjudication found 6.2%. Newer follow-ups inside the last 30 days include 'Beyond Majority Vote' (arXiv:2609.03953, Findings of EMNLP 2026) arguing single-pass hallucination benchmarks undercount errors, and 'When Rubrics Fail' (arXiv:2609.12718) finding that rubric scores often miss clinician-relevant hallucinations and that retrieval-based factuality checks recover some rubric-blind errors; on the mitigation side, HDSR/HDSR-PL (arXiv:2605.28910) reduces clinical-summary hallucinations 24-48% in Llama-3.1-8B on MIMIC-IV-Note v2.2. Two structural pressures matter for MediKiosk: the most influential 2026 evaluation work is largely vendor-authored (Composo sells evaluation tooling; Augnito documents clinical notes; Bergman et al. are vendor-affiliated), so the numbers carry conflicts of interest and should be cited with provenance; and India's ABDM/NRCeS ecosystem has no equivalent omission/hallucination benchmark targeted at ABDM output, meaning Module C would be building a per-field, NRCeS-aware harness that no competitor in this cluster supplies.

history.release_date: Augnito paper: first released as arXiv:2604.14829, 'Beyond Literal Summarization: Redefining Hallucination for Medical SOAP Note Evaluation', submitted 16 Apr 2026 (v1 only). Omission paper: first released as arXiv:2608.31016, 'LLM Judges Verify Presence, Not Absence: Omission Blindness in AI Clinical Notes and What Recovers It', submitted 31 Aug 2026 (v1 only), released concurrently with its companion census arXiv:2608.31017, 'One note in three', likewise submitted 31 Aug 2026 (v1 only).
history.key_milestones: 2023-11: MED-OMIT (arXiv:2311.08303) establishes fact-enumeration for omission measurement in medical summarisation, the omission paper's direct ancestor. 2024-12-17: Composo closes its USD 2.0M pre-seed (Twin Path Ventures, JVH Ventures, EWOR). 2025: AbsenceBench (Fu et al.) establishes the general language-model absence-detection gap; Composo continues its judge-reliability campaign (a RewardBench 2 study on five judge techniques reported Apr 2026). 2026-04-16: Augnito Research posts arXiv:2604.14829 claiming 35.2% lexical versus 9.1% inference-aware hallucination rates against a 10.4% human baseline. 2026-04: DeLucia et al. (arXiv:2604.16383) and Hussain et al. (arXiv:2604.06216) post concurrent judge-reliability work. 2026-04-27: Augnito's paper is promoted publicly on LinkedIn. 2026-05-10: the independent Pith T0 review raises two load-bearing objections to the Augnito paper; the authors respond 'revision: yes' but no revised version is posted. 2026-07: Dahlberg et al. publish their systematic review of note-evaluation methods in Artificial Intelligence in Medicine. 2026-08-14: the omission paper's physician author validates 70 items across six stages. 2026-08-17: an independent clinician blind-grades the severity rubric in a 24-item sitting. 2026-08-17/21: Bergman et al. post their pre-registered judge-validation and five-country paired studies on medRxiv. 2026-08-31: OmissionBench (arXiv:2608.31016) and the companion census (arXiv:2608.31017) are released together, with the dataset and MIT-licensed harness. 2026-09-02: the omission paper circulates on Hacker News and in news summaries. 2026-09-03: 'Beyond Majority Vote' (arXiv:2609.03953) is posted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 2026-09-11: 'When Rubrics Fail' (arXiv:2609.12718) is posted.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: Inside the six-month window (approximately 2026-03-16 to 2026-09-16): the Augnito paper appeared on 16 Apr 2026 and has not been revised since, despite the May 2026 review request, so its status is stalled at a contested v1. The omission paper and its companion census both appeared on 31 Aug 2026 as v1 preprints with released data and code, and the benchmark's data version is tagged 'factorial-v1' with no v2. The omission paper's own construction records activity through 17 Aug 2026 (the independent severity-rubric sitting), and it cites concurrent work from April, July and August 2026 (DeLucia, Dahlberg, Hussain, Bergman, MED-OMIT-adjacent CARE), showing the field moving underneath it. Newer, independent follow-ups within the last ~30 days of the verification date: 'Beyond Majority Vote' (3 Sep 2026, Findings of EMNLP 2026) on multi-perspective adjudication and benchmark undercounting; 'When Rubrics Fail' (11 Sep 2026) on rubric blind spots and retrieval-based factuality recovery; and HDSR/HDSR-PL (2 Jun 2026) on detector-guided hallucination reduction for clinical summarisation. No new version, errata, retraction, peer-reviewed venue acceptance or direct citing paper for arXiv:2604.14829 was found; the only substantive external engagement with it located in this sweep is the Pith review and its being cited by the omission paper as the comparator result 'pointing the other way'.

market_positioning.target_users: The omission work targets evaluators and buyers of ambient-scribe/AI-note quality: vendor quality and safety teams, hospital and health-system procurement and clinical-safety reviewers, regulators looking for an audit instrument, and clinical-NLP researchers. The Augnito work targets clinical-NLP researchers, model evaluators and vendors arguing about what should count as a hallucination in clinical documentation. Neither targets patients, and neither is packaged for direct clinical deployment.
market_positioning.market_segment: Clinical-note evaluation methodology and AI-output quality assurance: benchmarks, judge designs, error taxonomies and audit instruments for AI-generated clinical documentation. It sits upstream of clinical documentation products (ambient scribes, summarisers) and adjacent to the broader LLM-evaluation-platform market that Composo competes in.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: The omission paper positions itself in its own words around a single claim - 'judges verify presence, not absence' - and argues that 'what recovers detection is restructuring the task: list the facts the transcript establishes, then verify each one against the note as a closed presence check', releasing the benchmark, prompts and judgements so others can attack the remaining open problem (restatement-trace omissions). The companion census pitches the instrument side: 'a failure rate depends on the instrument as much as the scribes', with the review instruction alone moving the verified share of candidates from 9.3% to 79.0%. Composo as a company pitches a calibrated quality layer that 'catches AI mistakes and publishes their numbers', deployed in 2-4 weeks and calibrated to a customer's own failure taxonomy. The Augnito paper positions itself against over-literal evaluation, arguing that 'naive hallucination detection which flags any claim not explicitly stated in a source transcript dramatically overestimates hallucination rates in SOAP note generation, conflating clinically valid inference with fabrication', and that the field needs 'evaluation standards that are simultaneously rigorous in their demand for factual fidelity and sophisticated in their understanding of what clinical documentation actually requires'.
